 The diesel squeeze: Rising fuel costs put the global potato supply chain under pressure
 on October 22, 2026 
 From North American harvest fields to European processing hubs and Southern Hemisphere planting operations, expensive diesel is tightening margins across the potato industry. Government intervention is cushioning some businesses, but growers, contractors and transport operators face sharply different levels of protection. 
 By Lukie Pieterse , Editor and Publisher of Potato News Today
 Information current to October 22, 2026. Prices are reported in their original currencies. Road-diesel benchmarks, agricultural fuel prices and wholesale prices are identified separately; they do not represent equivalent costs to farmers. 
 Rising diesel costs are adding another layer of financial pressure to the international potato industry, increasing the expense of field operations and crop transport while complicating decisions about contracts, working capital and the next planting season.
 The pressure is visible across several major producing regions. U.S. road diesel remains substantially above year-earlier levels. Canadian farm organisations report sharply higher harvest expenses. British and Irish growers face expensive fuel during lifting, while Australian potato producers have cited diesel costs amid difficult processing-contract negotiations. South African industry analysis highlights the particular vulnerability of developing potato producers.
 The picture nevertheless varies considerably between countries. Some prices have eased from recent peaks, and government measures have moderated the immediate impact in several markets. India’s state-owned retailers and China’s latest pricing decision illustrate why a global diesel shock does not translate into identical price movements everywhere.
 For potato businesses, the central issue is how much of the additional cost they must absorb—and whether their selling prices, contracts and cash reserves can accommodate it.
 A diesel supply problem with consequences beyond the pump 
 The International Energy Agency’s October Oil Market Report identifies prolonged disruption to Middle Eastern and Russian supplies as a major source of pressure. Global diesel exports in September were approximately 700,000 barrels a day below year-earlier levels, with increased shipments from other suppliers failing to compensate fully for the losses.
 Although international diesel prices had retreated from September’s exceptional highs, the IEA reported that benchmarks remained close to twice their pre-crisis levels. Refinery constraints, expensive shipping and depleted inventories were continuing to strain the market ahead of Northern Hemisphere winter demand.
 The agency has urged member governments to accelerate outstanding emergency stock releases, prioritising diesel, and to consider whether additional releases are warranted. These measures can provide a buffer, but their effectiveness depends on the volumes, timing and location of deliveries.
 For potato growers, the timing of the disruption matters. Fuel-intensive work follows crop development, soil conditions and weather windows. Delaying a necessary operation until diesel becomes cheaper may carry costs of its own.
 United States: Harvest costs rise, while potato-sector relief remains uncertain 
 The U.S. Energy Information Administration reported a national average on-highway diesel price of US$6.276 per gallon for October 19. That was 9.7 cents higher than the previous week and US$2.656 above the comparable year-earlier level—an increase of approximately 73%.
 Regional differences were substantial. The Rocky Mountain average stood at US$6.422 per gallon, while the West Coast average excluding California was US$6.659. These are road-fuel prices including taxes, rather than quotations for farm-delivered, off-road diesel. They are nevertheless significant benchmarks for businesses moving potatoes, inputs and finished products by truck.
 Washington has responded with an announced US$8 billion Harvest Fuel Relief programme. USDA’s October 19 statement said payments would cover part of modelled losses during the 2026 crop year.
 The distinction for potato growers is important: USDA said commodity-specific rates for Title I crops would be released in November, while payment methodology for other eligible commodities would follow later. Specialty-crop producers were invited to submit information about increased fuel costs. The announcement therefore does not establish a potato-specific payment rate or guarantee reimbursement of individual growers’ diesel bills.
 Separate federal measures concerning highway use of dyed diesel have also encountered practical limitations. Reuters reported on October 22 that state taxes and restrictions, fuel availability and concerns about dye remaining in vehicle tanks were discouraging some users. For potato transport businesses, the practical benefit depends on applicable state requirements and their existing fuel arrangements.
 Canada: Tax concessions offer limited insulation from higher fuel costs 
 The Ontario Federation of Agriculture (OFA) has provided a striking illustration of the increase in farm fuel expenditure.
 In an October 14 commentary, OFA Vice-President Sara Wood estimated that filling a modern combine’s approximately 1,250-litre tank had risen from about C$1,560 last autumn to more than C$2,600 this year. The federation calculated that a representative 500-acre corn, soybean and wheat farm could face more than C$14,000 in additional annual diesel costs.
 These are examples from other cropping systems, rather than potato cost estimates. They demonstrate the scale of the broader agricultural fuel shock.
 OFA also stressed that eligible agricultural machinery already uses tax-exempt coloured diesel, yet its price has increased sharply. The organisation warned that expenses rising faster than farm receipts leave less money for maintenance, investment and the following season.
 For Canadian potato businesses, the implication is a need to assess field fuel and road haulage separately. A farm’s machinery fuel arrangements may differ from those of the contractor delivering seed, hauling the harvested crop or transporting potatoes to a processor.
 Britain and Ireland: Expensive diesel meets the demands of lifting 
 Britain’s National Farmers’ Union reported on October 21 that UK diesel was averaging approximately £2.00 per litre. That road-fuel figure should be distinguished from agricultural red-diesel quotations.
 The NFU nevertheless made clear that farming remains exposed. Deputy President Paul Tompkins identified red diesel as the principal fuel for agricultural vehicles and warned that rising costs were intensifying financial pressure after a difficult, drought-affected season. The union is seeking measures to support farm cash flow and investment.
 Ireland provides direct evidence from the potato sector. In its October 7 potato market report, the Irish Farmers’ Association said the impact of high diesel prices was particularly evident during harvest, when fuel consumption increases significantly.
 The report also described variable yields and dry lifting conditions elsewhere in Europe. In eastern Britain, extending towards Yorkshire, some fields required irrigation before lifting. These observations were specific to the early-October reporting period.
 For growers, the combination can be costly: machinery and transport bills must be met even when marketable yield disappoints. Where irrigation uses diesel-powered pumping, preparing dry ground for lifting can add another direct fuel expense.
 Continental Europe: Elevated prices across the processing heartland 
 Germany, France, the Netherlands and Belgium face differing fuel-tax arrangements and agricultural support measures, but published road-diesel benchmarks show substantial increases across all four countries.
 GlobalPetrolPrices’ October 19 figures provide the following snapshot:
 Country Road-diesel benchmark Change from one year earlier 
 Germany €2.27/litre +41.9% 
 France €2.35/litre +47.8% 
 Netherlands €2.48/litre +46.7% 
 Belgium €2.37/litre +45.4% 
 Source: GlobalPetrolPrices, October 19, 2026. These are published retail benchmarks, rather than growers’ net agricultural fuel costs after applicable relief or commercial discounts. 
 The figures also show why the direction of travel needs careful description. German diesel was 7% below its month-earlier level; France and Belgium had recorded smaller monthly declines, while the Dutch benchmark was unchanged. Prices remained elevated despite this partial easing.
 Germany has temporarily reduced energy taxes on petrol and diesel from October 1 through December 31. The government puts the reduction at approximately 14 euro cents per litre before the associated VAT effect, or around 17 cents including VAT. It also states that the agricultural diesel refund has been fully reinstated. Those arrangements must be considered when assessing actual farm costs.
 France has continued more targeted assistance. A government announcement extended agricultural fuel support of 15 euro cents per litre through September and October. The same announcement said fuel assistance for transport operators had ended in August and noted that fuel-cost changes were being reflected in transport invoices.
 For the interconnected potato industries of France, Belgium, Germany and the Netherlands, this creates several potential points of exposure. Growers face machinery costs; contractors must recover operating expenses; processors and packers face inbound and outbound freight charges.
 The commercial effect will depend on delivery distances, fuel-adjustment clauses, purchasing arrangements and who bears each transport cost. A national pump price alone cannot establish the increase in a grower’s cost per tonne.
 India: State retailers cushion consumers, while private prices diverge 
 India’s experience illustrates the role of domestic pricing policy.
 Reuters reported on October 16 that state-owned Indian Oil, Bharat Petroleum and Hindustan Petroleum had left pump prices unchanged since May, absorbing substantial losses on diesel sales. Private retailers had raised prices, encouraging some customers to move to state-run outlets.
 The same report identified agricultural demand, including diesel-powered irrigation, alongside stronger festival-related trucking activity.
 For price context, an October 16 city survey published by Mint listed diesel at ₹95.20 per litre in New Delhi, ₹95.36 in Lucknow and ₹99.82 in Kolkata. These were city retail quotations, rather than a single national agricultural fuel price.
 For potato producers and traders, relatively stable prices at state outlets provide a degree of short-term protection. However, the purchasing channel matters, as do transport charges and reliance on diesel-powered equipment.
 A flat pump price during one period also does not mean that the business is insulated from the wider cost shock. Costs can emerge through machinery services, logistics or subsequent pricing decisions.
 China: The latest pricing decision points to stability 
 China’s most recent reported decision was to keep retail gasoline and diesel prices unchanged from October 16, according to Reuters, citing the National Development and Reform Commission.
 That provides a useful distinction within the global picture. The latest international supply pressure did not produce an immediate retail increase at that adjustment.
 For the potato sector, the decision offers a measure of near-term price stability. It does not, by itself, establish individual farms’ delivered fuel costs or prove that transport and other operating expenses are unchanged.
 Australia: Fuel pressure becomes part of the potato-contract debate 
 Australia offers one of the clearest current examples of diesel costs entering a potato-sector dispute.
 TasFarmers said in early October that McCain was seeking an A$15-per-tonne reduction in processing-potato prices. Growers’ committee chair Glynn Williams cited diesel approaching A$3 per litre among the pressures facing producers preparing to plant.
 McCain disputed the suggestion that discussions had stopped. Potato Business reported that the company said conversations with growers were continuing in good faith and that pricing negotiations were commercially sensitive. These statements describe the positions reported in early October; they do not establish the eventual contract outcome.
 Broader fuel data confirm the scale of the operating environment. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission reported average retail diesel of 278.5 Australian cents per litre across the five largest cities on October 14. That was 2.5 cents lower than a week earlier, but 101.9 cents above February 20.
 Across more than 190 regional locations, the corresponding average was 284.1 cents per litre.
 The Australian Institute of Petroleum subsequently reported a national average retail diesel price of 280.7 cents per litre for the week ending October 18. Its wholesale benchmark was 261.3 cents. These indicators provide market context; farm bulk contracts and applicable fuel-tax credits affect the final cost to individual operators.
 The potato-contract question is therefore immediate: how can growers maintain viable margins when an important operating cost rises while the proposed price for their crop falls?
 New Zealand: A substantial annual increase 
 Stats NZ reported on October 16 that diesel prices had increased in September and stood 55.8% above their level a year earlier.
 For potato businesses, this points to exposure through field machinery, contracting and road transport. Individual outcomes will depend on fuel purchasing arrangements and the extent to which service providers adjust charges.
 New Zealand’s fuel-security response also remains relevant. The Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment continues to publish information on the country’s response to supply disruption, making availability and resilience part of the operating picture alongside price.
 South Africa: Another increase compounds pressure on vulnerable growers 
 South Africa’s October adjustment delivered a further substantial increase.
 The government raised the diesel price by R2.8438 per litre for 0.05% sulphur fuel and R3.2438 for 0.005% sulphur fuel, effective October 7. These are increases in the administered diesel price structure, rather than a uniform retail quotation at every outlet.
 The government attributed the adjustment to international petroleum prices, supply shortages, shipping costs and other factors.
 Potatoes SA had already documented the vulnerability of developing growers in an analysis published on May 20. Author Rachichi Marokane described how earlier fuel increases, weather disruption and weak returns from preceding crops had combined to constrain producers.
 That report linked expensive diesel to higher machinery and contractor costs and, in some cases, reduced planting. It also emphasised that the timing of fuel increases relative to field operations influenced the severity of the impact. Those findings concern the earlier part of the 2026 season, rather than an assessment of October’s adjustment.
 The latest increase adds to an already difficult cost environment. For businesses with limited working capital, the immediate challenge can be financing essential operations before revenue from the crop arrives.
 Storage, processing and transport face different forms of exposure 
 The evidence from these markets points to several implications across the potato supply chain.
 For growers and contractors, the most direct exposure is fuel consumed during fieldwork, harvesting and crop movement. For packers and processors, transport costs can enter through raw-potato deliveries, inputs and finished-product distribution. The French government’s account of fuel-cost adjustments appearing in freight invoices demonstrates one route by which the increase moves downstream.
 Storage requires a more precise distinction. Ventilation and refrigeration are major electricity uses, so a percentage increase in diesel cannot simply be applied to the entire storage-energy bill. Diesel remains relevant where facilities use it for transport, handling equipment or backup generation.
 Research published in the Journal of Food Process Engineering identifies refrigeration performance, insulation, air infiltration and operational management as important influences on potato cold-storage energy demand.
 For processors, the same discipline applies: diesel exposure should be assessed separately from electricity, gas and other energy inputs. Higher haulage costs may affect a factory even where its processing equipment uses different energy sources.
 The practical calculation is consequently business-specific. As North Dakota State University’s potato-budget guidance explains, enterprise budgets are models that must be adapted to individual conditions, with considerable variation between farms.
 The pressure extends to next season’s decisions 
 The IEA expects constrained middle-distillate supplies to persist into 2027. Its October assessment indicates that rebuilding depleted inventories will take time, even if refinery activity recovers. That is a forecast subject to supply, demand and geopolitical developments, rather than a fixed timetable for diesel prices.
 For potato businesses, the evidence supports updating budgets with current delivered-fuel quotations, realistic machinery use and actual transport terms. Relief programmes, tax refunds and fuel-adjustment clauses can materially change the result.
 The longer-term concern is investment capacity. OFA’s warning that rising expenses reduce funds available for maintenance and future production has relevance well beyond Ontario. The Tasmanian negotiations similarly show how fuel costs can become part of a broader debate about grower viability.
 The present diesel squeeze therefore reaches beyond the cost of completing this season’s work. It is influencing the financial room available to prepare for the next one—and the ability of growers, contractors, hauliers and processors to keep the potato supply chain functioning profitably.
